## What changed

Two things, in two different runs, in opposite directions. This task is the clearest example in the
branch of a candidate genuinely breaking something and a later candidate genuinely fixing it.

**Iteration 1 (`run_20260816_202942`) broke it outright.** Its `cand_0001` — a retry rule plus a
degraded-report rule plus a narrowing of the `get_job_log` instruction — scored **0.000 on all three
val trials** against a seed of `0.967`. `results/v2/per_task_scores.csv` records it as
**"REAL regression from candidate,"** and that label is correct: three trials, three zeros, no
harness errors. A zero here means the gate failed — no completion, or no usable answer at all. That
candidate was rejected (val `0.834`, Δ `−0.042`) and the champion stayed the seed.

**Iteration 2 (`run_20260818_161550`) recovered it.** The accepted `cand_0001` rewrote the rule that
mattered for this task. The seed said:

> **Don't re-fetch job data.** If a prior `query_aap2` call already returned job metadata or events,
> extract what you need… Do NOT make a redundant second call to the same job.

The champion says:

> **Don't re-fetch the SAME fields.** … Calling `get_job` AND `get_job_log` on the same job is NOT
> re-fetching: they return DIFFERENT fields (metadata vs. log text) and are complementary.

This task's contract expects **two** tool calls on the same job. The seed's own rule forbade the
second one.

## What worked

`cand_0001` scored **0.978** at `n=9` — seven trials at `1.000`, two at `0.900` — against a seed of
**0.800** at the same `n=9`. A gain of **+0.178** at equal `n`.

The decomposition is unambiguous and it lands exactly on the edited rule. With weights
`0.2 / 0.8`, two expected calls and two required facts:

| observed | expected calls matched | answer facts | trials |
|--:|:--|:--|--:|
| 0.800 | **0 of 2** | 2 of 2 | 8 (seed @ n=9) |
| 0.900 | 1 of 2 | 2 of 2 | 2 (`cand_0001`) |
| 1.000 | **2 of 2** | 2 of 2 | 7 (`cand_0001`) |

**The seed got both answer facts right on every single valid trial and earned zero tool-call
credit on every single one.** It knew which Ansible task failed and on which host; it just never made
the two-call sequence the contract wanted, because its own Rule 4 told it not to. The champion moved
seven of nine trials to full call coverage without touching the answer component at all.

That is a rule-level fix with a rule-level effect, visible in the right column of the reward. It is
the cleanest confirmation in v2 that the reward's `tool_calls` term is doing the discriminating.

## What didn't

**The reported delta for this task is `+0.011`, and it is meaningless.** It compares the `n=9`
candidate against a *reused* `n=3` `seed` of `0.967` (`[0.900, 1.000, 1.000]`) that was never
re-measured in this run. At `n=9` the seed is `0.800`. The real effect is sixteen times the reported
one.

**The seed also lost a trial the candidate did not.** Position 5 of its `n=9` vector is a
`NetworkConnectionError` — one of the two such errors in this run, both at index 5, both in
`seed_train` cells. Counting it as a zero would report the seed at `0.711` and inflate the gain to
`+0.267`. That figure is biased in the candidate's favour and is not the one to quote.

**And iteration 1's regression was never diagnosed.** Its journal entry proposed exactly the right
next step — "if reject-broke-passing, back off Rule 6 to fire only after a retried tool error (already
the case)" and "isolate which of Rules 5/6/`get_job_log`-narrowing regressed and redesign only that
one." The framework's `RESULT` line named this task under `broke={}`. But the iteration-2 optimizer
wrote **no handover at all** (`## Iteration cand_0001 — (no handover written by the optimizer)`), so
there is no record of whether the recovery was deliberate or incidental. Three zeros on a task is the
most informative signal either run produced, and the reason for them is not written down anywhere.

## What we can (or can't) learn

**We can learn that this task's difficulty, as scored, is a two-call sequencing requirement — and
that the seed skill actively prohibited satisfying it.** The scenario was authored to discriminate
agents that report the *first* host they encounter (`stor-node-01`, which succeeded) from those that
report the host where the failure occurred (`stor-node-02`). Measured, the seed passes that test on
every valid trial. The discrimination the contract actually performed was a different one, and an
accidental one: whether the agent's instructions let it call two complementary actions on the same
job.

**We can learn that a rejected candidate's damage is recoverable and worth chasing.** Iteration 1's
zeros here are the strongest evidence in v2 that the gate does useful work — it caught a real,
total regression on a real task and reverted it. That is the same mean-based paired gate that
discarded v1's only trajectory match (see [`v1-aap2-0047`](v1-aap2-0047.md)). It is the right
mechanism pointed at the right question here and at the wrong question there.

**We cannot conclude the champion is safe on this task.** Two of its nine trials still lose a call,
and no rollout was read to find out which. And the underlying edit is, again, a correction to the
skill's description of the harness's tool behaviour rather than to its reasoning — the same
transferability question raised in [`v1`-vs-`v2` terms](../../results/v2/summary.md) and on
[`v2-bench-aap2-001`](v2-bench-aap2-001-single-job-outcome.md).
